children: By Andy Serwer
I am for the man who drives a hammer...I am for the revolution's coming
-'Manifesto' by Roxy Music
Somewhere, (yes, probably somewhere hot), Karl Marx is smiling.

The co-author of the Communist Manifesto, (along with Friedrich Engels) must be delighted at the recent spate of manifestos being handed down by CEOs and other leading lights. Chief executives these days, especially in Silicon Valley, seem compelled to share their thoughts in essays put out for the rest of us to consume.

What perhaps began with Moses, continued to Martin Luther, and then to Marx has now been handed down to...Leopold Aschenbrenner. The latter, you may recall, runs the Situational Awareness hedge fund which presumably takes its name from Aschenbrenner's 165-page essay, 'Situational Awareness The Decade Ahead,' published in June 2024. My favorite part is in the very beginning, where he writes: "...right now, there are perhaps a few hundred people, most of them in San Francisco and the AI labs, that have situational awareness. Through whatever peculiar forces of fate, I have found myself among them."

Though I view Aschenbrenner's statement as contradictory, apparently others found it compelling enough to invest billions of dollars in Leo's fund, which recently semi-crashed and was saved from a worse fate by Ken Griffin's Citadel. (The irony of it all spawned a bit of commentary on X.)

Marc ('Software is eating the world') Andreessen was early to call these pieces 'manifestos' with his 2023 The Techno-Optimist Manifesto, which seemed to open the floodgates. Most recent was Bill Gates' nearly 6,000 word opus on AI put forth last Wednesday. It's worth reading I guess, although not all of it is new or surprising, and it does go on. Verbosity seems to be seen as a virtue here, (the Communist Manifesto by the way checks in at 11,468 words), a trend I've complained about in the writing of CEO shareholder letters, which have become manifestos in themselves.

Sadly, what Gates suggests as solutions to the problems that AI may generate (unemployment or its use by bad actors), which are taxes on AI tokens and robots and national and global leaders coalescing to form interdisciplinary, oversight bodies, don't seem particularly feasible. It's also not clear to me why Gates waited until now to weigh in.

A few weeks before Gates, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg released his 6,500 word essay, "The Future is for Everyone." This one has a few lines that left me scratching my head, like: "I don't understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity's relevance would rush to build that future." (Because they would make money, Zuck.)
And this: "The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic." (That's not the only means to safeguard.)

In October of 2024 Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, put out a 13,000 word treatise he called "Machines of Loving Grace." Amodei gets his title from a poem by American counterculture icon Richard Brautigan, "All Watched Over By Machines Of Loving Grace," which Brautigan wrote in 1967 (the same year he published "Trout Fishing in America") while a poet-in-residence at the California Institute of Technology. Amodie's is the most literary and arguably intellectual of these, with 29 footnotes.

Amodei's rival, Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, has written a series of essays over the past two years, The Intelligence Age, The Gentle Singularity and Industrial Policy for the Intelligence Age, the latter having some of the same ideas Gates put forth about government needing to step up.

At just over 800 words, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's manifesto from this June, 'A frontier without an ecosystem isn't stable', is a comparative haiku. In it Nadella warns of a few AI models that "eat [that word again] everything they see. Think about what happened in the first phase of globalization where entire industrial economies were hollowed out by outsourcing. The GDP numbers looked fine on the surface, but the displacement was real and the consequences are still being felt."

In a slightly different vein, I should mention super-investor Stan Druckenmiller's recent manifesto, actually an OpEd in The Wall Street Journal. I bring up Druck's piece because it engendered a fierce little debate after it was discovered that he used AI to write it. Why not, Druckenmiller said, it's like using a calculator for math. He also said "The only embarrassing thing is how many people reached out and told me how much better written this was than normal."

I could argue either side of this. There's the point about CEOs using ghost writers. And increasingly many of us are using AI. For writers, it's a question of degree I suppose. As a sounding board, or to make some queries, OK. But asking AI to gin up an entire essay or story and post it without review, that's very different.

Which brings me back to the manifestos. How many of these and/or how much of them were written by machine, not man? What about Amodei's? Did he use Claude? Wouldn't it be almost an indictment of his own product if he didn't? (Or worse yet, if he used ChatGPT!) "I used Claude to give me ideas, and to help with the research, but the actual writing is mine," Amodei told NBC. "I don't think Claude is quite good enough yet to write the whole thing but I definitely used it to improve my ideas."

Actually in his essay Amodie gives a shout-out to a number of prominent humans: "Thanks to Kevin Esvelt, Parag Mallick, Stuart Ritchie, Matt Yglesias, Erik Brynjolfsson, Jim McClave, Allan Dafoe, and many people at Anthropic for reviewing drafts of this essay." Aschenbrenner does this as well.

To me what's most important when it comes to these manifestos, AI-aided or not, is readability. Some go on and on, or are repetitive or just dull. If AI can help this cohort make their points better, fine. (Try: 'make this 50% shorter and livelier!') It's also worth considering what Nick Thompson, CEO of the Atlantic said recently when making the case against using AI for writing. Thompson suggested, among other points, that the very process of writing is thinking which allows for furthering and elevating an argument.
True that.

In Bill Gates's essay he mentions Pope Leo XIV's encyclical from May on AI, "On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence." The Pope focuses on AI in Chapter Three: TECHNOLOGY AND DOMINANCE.  THE GRANDEUR OF HUMANITY IN LIGHT OF THE PROMISES OF AI . If AI is used as a force for good, then it will be "akin to the rebuilding of Jerusalem narrated in the Book of Nehemiah" the pontiff writes. "If, however, power grows while the heart withers and human bonds fray, then we are faced with a new form of Babel-a construction that is grandiose, yet fundamentally dehumanizing."
Now here's a guy who's entitled to write encyclicals-or manifestos for that matter.
(AI didn't write this 1,130 or so word piece.)
